long_articles.title: Apple TV Started at $69 in 2015
long_articles.summary: Apple CEO Tim Cook on Monday at the “Spring Forward” media event in San Francisco announced that Apple TV will now cost $69, discounted from its regular price of $99. The new price for the set-top box
long_articles.content:
Apple CEO Tim Cook on Monday at the “Spring Forward” media event in San Francisco announced that Apple TV will now cost $69, discounted from its regular price of $99. The new price for the set-top box arrives on the heels of the announcement of [HBO Now for Apple TV](https://www.macrumors.com/2015/03/09/hbo-now-apple-tv/). The new price appears to apply to the third-generation Apple TV, as the company did not announce a new set-top box on stage at the Yerba Buena Center this afternoon. 

![Apple TV 69](https://images.macrumors.com/t/09MEyjMv3pwahNK5JknROk0B2A8=/400x0/article-new/2015/03/Apple-TV-69-800x356.jpg?lossy)
A revamped Apple TV has been rumored to be in the works for quite some time, but the next-generation set-top box is not expected to be announced until later this year or beyond. The upcoming Apple TV is expected to have an improved, tactile remote control and a brand new operating system with a built-in App Store. New apps are also expected to have redesigned user interfaces.

Follow the rest of our [March 2015 event coverage](https://www.macrumors.com/roundup/march-2015-event/) for the latest information.

long_articles.title: The Late Charlie Munger on Elon Musk and Tesla
long_articles.summary: Owning Tesla stock has been a bit of a roller coaster ride as of late: During the first week of February, for example, the stock had "one of its wildest weeks ever," [CNBC reported](https://www.cnbc.c
long_articles.content:
Owning Tesla stock has been a bit of a roller coaster ride as of late: During the first week of February, for example, the stock had "one of its wildest weeks ever," [CNBC reported](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/06/tesla-becomes-top-holding-on-sofi-as-young-investors-clamor-into-stock.html), with the share price "swinging hundreds of dollars in both directions." On Thursday, when Tesla announced it will sell [2.65 million new shares](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/14/tesla-prices-its-secondary-offering-at-767-a-share.html) of stock, the share price jumped [nearly 5%](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/13/tesla-shares-fall-after-company-announces-2-billion-common-stock-offering.html). After it announced the new stock will sell at [$767 a share](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/14/tesla-prices-its-secondary-offering-at-767-a-share.html) on Friday, the stock fell [2%](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/14/tesla-prices-its-secondary-offering-at-767-a-share.html) in premarket trading.

At the [annual shareholders meeting for newspaper company Daily Journal ](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/12/watch-berkshire-hathaways-charlie-munger-speaks-at-the-daily-journal-annual-meeting.html)on Wednesday, a shareholder asked Berkshire Hathaway vice chairman Munger what he thought about Musk, based on Tesla's recent ups and downs.

"My thoughts are two," Munger, who serves as the Journal's chairman replied. "I would never buy [Tesla], and I would never sell it short," he said, referring to a technique investors use to bet that a stock will decline.

And "I have a third comment," the billionaire investor continued: "Never underestimate the man who overestimates himself. I think Elon Musk is peculiar and he may overestimate himself, but he may not be wrong all the time."

At the Daily Journal's 2019 shareholder meeting, Munger shared similar thoughts, but also said that he personally [would not hire](https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2019/02/19/charlie-munger-ideal-hire-wouldnt-be-someone-like-elon-musk.html) Musk.

"I want the guy who understands his limitations instead of the guy who doesn't," Munger said at the time. "On the other hand, I've learned something terribly important in life…. These weird guys who overestimate themselves occasionally knock it right out of the park.

"I don't want my personal life to be [around] a bunch of guys who are living in a state of delusion, who happen occasionally to win big. I want the prudent person," Munger explained.

Musk and Tesla did not immediately respond to CNBC Make It's request for comment.

Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway chairman and Munger's longtime business partner, has also given his opinion on Musk.

"He's trying to do something to improve a product, and I salute him for that," Buffett said on [CNBC's "Squawk Box"](https://www.cnbc.com/2018/05/07/warren-buffett-i-salute-elon-musk-for-trying-to-improve-a-product.html) in May 2018. It's "not easy" to do that, Buffett said. "The American public will decide whether [Tesla's electric cars are] a success."

Currently, Tesla's market cap is [over $140 billion](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/TSLA), first hitting the [$100 billion mark](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/01/22/tesla-reaches-100-billion-market-cap.html) in January.

According to [Musk's compensation package](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/01/14/as-tesla-shares-rise-elon-musk-stands-to-reap-a-346-million-payout.html), if Tesla stock hits $3,665, the company's profit target hits $14 billion a year and other financial targets are met, Musk will get more than $55 billion. With the added value to Tesla and Musk's personal payday,** **that would make his total net worth over $175 billion, [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/04/tesla-ceo-elon-musk-got-4point5-billion-richer-overnight.html) [reported](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/04/tesla-ceo-elon-musk-got-4point5-billion-richer-overnight.html). Jeff Bezos, the richest person in the world, currently has a net worth of $131 billion, according to [Bloomberg's Billionaires Index](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/).

Right now, Musk is the 24th richest person in the world, according to the index, with a net worth of $41.1 billion. Buffett is worth $89 billion, the index shows, and Munger is worth $2 billion, according to [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/profile/charles-munger/#56b572bb697a).

With Friday's Tesla announcement, Musk pledged to buy $10 million in shares Tesla's secondary stock offering. Board member Larry Ellison will buy $1 million in shares, the electric car company said.

long_articles.title: ★ HomeView Thoughts and Observations
long_articles.summary: I’ll start with a nomenclatural sidenote: Apple seems to be going with “Apple HomeView” as the product’s name. E.g., the URL slug for it on Apple.com is *[apple-homeview/](https://www.apple.com/apple-
long_articles.content:
I’ll start with a nomenclatural sidenote: Apple seems to be going with “Apple HomeView” as the product’s name. E.g., the URL slug for it on Apple.com is *[apple-homeview/](https://www.apple.com/apple-homeview/)*, not just *homeview/*. Few people notice and no one who doesn’t work in Apple product marketing cares, but they actually do the same thing with Vision Pro — in Cupertino, it’s “Apple Vision Pro” (once again including [the URL slug](https://www.apple.com/apple-vision-pro/)). Yet this week’s new HomePod Mini is just “[HomePod mini 2](https://www.apple.com/homepod-mini/)” and the existing 2nd-generation HomePod is just “[HomePod (2nd generation)](https://www.apple.com/homepod-2nd-generation/)” — not “HomePod 2” or “Apple HomePod”. I certainly intend to just call it “HomeView”.

Apple introduced HomeView with a three-minute introductory film simulating a suburban family’s hectic before-school/work kitchen rush hour, with versions hosted [on Apple’s site](https://www.apple.com/105/media/us/apple-homeview/2026/f7ce47a8-10f2-455c-b99f-bf9b85a35cb6/films/product/apple-homeview-product-tpl-us-2026_16x9.m3u8) and [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hkrYiZ_g9tw). The most ridiculous aspect of it is that anyone would possibly make their kid French toast in that scenario. I’d have told my son to make his own goddamn French toast with that attitude. Or I’d have made a single serving and eaten it myself right in front of him. Bro.

I do think the basic concept is an intriguing idea. But as an implementation of that concept, my initial impressions are threefold. First, I am unconvinced that anyone in a family would use this for anything other than playing music or podcasts, rather than just using their phones. And if that’s the case, why not just have a HomePod? Apple’s video shows family members taking turns to use the HomeView, rotating it on the kitchen island to face themselves. Why? Why does the mom check her calendar on this, rather than on her iPhone, while the dad is using it to follow a French toast recipe? There’s a real “*Why do we need this?*” question here and I don’t think Apple’s video answers it, at all. You need to think you want it if you’re going to buy it. And even if you already had a HomeView set up, I’m not sure how often you’d use it instead of your phone, or instead of just talking to it like a screenless HomePod.

Second, all the touching and rotating — in Apple’s own demonstration — makes it seem awkward that HomeView must be tethered to a USB power cable. If you look closely in the video, they do show the USB power cable in some shots, but not many. And if you look really closely, this hypothetical family has drilled a hole in the center of their kitchen island to snake the cable through.

The hero shot introducing the product, of course, does not show the power cable at all:

[
  ![The “Introducing HomeView” title card shot from Apple’s video. It shows a HomeView sitting atop a kitchen island.](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-introducing.jpeg)](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-introducing.jpeg)

We see a wee bit of the cable when the dad reaches to touch the screen to start the French toast recipe:

[
  ![The HomeView, centered on the kitchen island, with about 2 inches of cable visible, disappearing into the island right behind the HomeView base.](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-cable-dad.jpeg)](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-cable-dad.jpeg)

And then a few seconds later, after the mom rotates the HomeView to the side, so she can check her calendar (despite the fact that she knows the dad was using it to follow a recipe), we get our most honest shot of the cabling situation:

[
  ![A view from behind the HomeView, which has been rotated to face the mom, showing about 4 inches of the USB cable disappearing into a convenient hole in the center of the island.](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-cable-mom-49s.jpeg)](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-cable-mom-49s.jpeg)

The above shot is at 0:49. It’s followed by two quick cuts to the dad and then the younger daughter, then at 0:52 we cut back to the mom (curious about her daughter’s new boyfriend situation), and, lo, the shot is now framed in such a way that we no longer see where the cable goes:

[
  ![Same view as the previous shot, except the camera has been tilted up about an inch, such that the cable just runs off the bottom of the frame, no longer showing that it disappears into a hole in the island that no kitchen island I’ve ever seen actually has.](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-cable-mom-52s.jpeg)](https://daringfireball.net/misc/2026/10/homeview-video-cable-mom-52s.jpeg)

If you think that slight reframing is happenstance, you should stay away from poker tables. Most kitchen islands I’m familiar with — including my own — have power outlets on the sides of the island. I’m sure some people have power outlets on the top surface of the counter, but I can’t recall seeing one. These are kitchen counters, not office desks. But either way, there’d be a long USB-C cable cluttering the countertop. And if you do happen to have a power outlet on the top surface of your counter, there’d be an adapter sticking out of it, all the time, to duplicate this HomeView setup.

This family’s convenient hole in the center of their island countertop is a fantasy. Where does the cable go underneath? How exactly do they have a power adapter plugged in down there? What happens when something spills on the counter? When we custom ordered our kitchen, we weren’t asked if we wanted any holes drilled in our island countertop, and if we *had* been asked, it would have made me wonder if the guy asking the question had a hole or two drilled in his head.

I know, it’s a marketing video. Marketing videos present products in ideal settings. But the power cable is an essential aspect of the standalone HomeView. I’m not suggesting that it should be battery powered. You’d still need to plug it in every few days, which would mean most people would just leave it plugged in, which gets us back to needing to live with an always-visible cable and power adapter in one of our living spaces. The countertop hole this cable disappears into in this video is less *ideal* and more *dishonest*.

The wall-mounted option seems more appealing to me, but now you’re talking about a home improvement project and (for most of us) calling an electrician. And that raises the question of why the wall-mounted version costs the same $300 as the one with the connected base, even though the base provides the subwoofer. And it requires a mount, and the mounts cost $60 (USB-C), $80 (AC wired), or $130 (PoE — and this one is not available yet). So the wall-mounted version, when you include a mount, costs more but sounds worse? This doesn’t make sense.

Those points make me skeptical that there’s a place for HomeView in my home. We have a stereo pair of HomePods in our kitchen. Neither is on the center island, because that would be dumb. They’re on the counters along the outside of the kitchen, each near an outlet on the wall. In the four days since HomeView was announced, I’ve tried to imagine when I’d want to look at something on a screen on either of them. My count remains at zero.

My third early impression is that the display is surprisingly small. I saw HomeView in person in New York on Tuesday, and I think Apple’s video conveys its size very accurately. It’s small and cute. It’s much more like a HomePod Mini with a screen than a full-size HomePod with a screen. For some reason I was expecting the latter. This is not a complaint, simply an observation. I actually think that making it small and cute makes it about as unobtrusive as an ever-present screen could possibly be. That’s good. But because it’s small you need to be close to it to read anything more detailed than large glanceable widgets.

The major difference between a device with a screen and one without is that you can watch video on a device with a screen. But HomeView clearly isn’t intended for that. It *can* play video but isn’t primarily *meant* to play video. If it were it would have a widescreen aspect ratio. But instead it has a square aspect ratio,[1](#fn1-2026-10-17) which is decidedly unsuited to video, unless, I suppose, you want a screen that is equally unsuited for both widescreen and tallscreen video.

So my skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me.

long_articles.title: Apple: ‘Strengthening App Review Guidelines Against Nonconsensual Intimate Imagery and Bait-And-Switch Apps’
long_articles.summary:
October 16, 2026

																			The App Review Guidelines are a core part of the safe and trusted experience that the App Store strives to offer users around the world — and the foundation of tha
long_articles.content:
October 16, 2026

																			The App Review Guidelines are a core part of the safe and trusted experience that the App Store strives to offer users around the world — and the foundation of that trust is clear standards that are consistently enforced. 

As outlined in our App Review Guidelines, pornographic material has long been prohibited on the App Store — this includes apps that generate nudity or sexually explicit imagery, such as “nudification” apps that create sexually explicit images of real individuals without their consent. Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch.

We want great apps and the innovative developers behind them to succeed on the App Store, and as new risks and novel user experiences emerge, we evolve our App Review Guidelines to maintain the trust of users and developers alike. Today we’re publishing updates that strengthen and extend the existing App Store protections, continuing to build on our long-held standards for privacy, quality, and safety.

For complete details, see the [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/).

### Changes

**1.2:** Content moderation requirements now explicitly cover nonconsensual intimate imagery — including imagery generated using AI tools — as content that apps must proactively prevent and remove from their platforms. Developers who fail to implement adequate safeguards — or don’t remedy violations after notice — risk violating the Developer Code of Conduct and being removed from the App Store.

**2.5.19:** This rule clarifies our longstanding prohibition on apps misrepresenting what they do during the App Review process and then changing after approval — for example, adding features or functionality that weren’t included in the version of the app that was submitted to App Review. Apps found engaging in this conduct are subject to removal from the App Store and removal from the Apple Developer Program.

**Section 5:** The App Store has always prohibited apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children (including child sexual abuse material). When we find instances of apps containing such content, we remove them from the App Store. We’ve updated Section 5 of the App Review guidelines to make clear that apps with such content will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.

We’re committed to keeping bad actors off the App Store, with established processes in place to review and act on apps that violate our guidelines. Last year, we prevented over 150K apps with safety issues from reaching customers and terminated over 193K developer accounts for engaging in fraud and abuse. These violations trace back to malicious actors — in some cases coordinated fraud operations — working to conceal harmful content that only becomes active once an app is approved, and as their tactics evolve, we continue to evolve our own tools and resources to prevent and catch this kind of behavior even faster. We do not hesitate to remove apps, and terminate the developers behind them, when they violate these guidelines.

long_articles.title: This Week in Package Management: 17 October 2026
long_articles.summary: This week’s package management news, gathered from the [package manager OPML feed collection](https://github.com/ecosyste-ms/package-managers-opml), my posts and boosts on [Mastodon](https://mastodon.
long_articles.content:
This week’s package management news, gathered from the [package manager OPML feed collection](https://github.com/ecosyste-ms/package-managers-opml), my posts and boosts on [Mastodon](https://mastodon.social/@andrewnez), and anything people sent me.

## Releases

[pnpm 12.12 to 12.14](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.14.0) add a `remoteCache` setting that shares signed task results and dependency builds through a pnpr server or any server that implements the Turborepo Remote Cache API, and 12.14 adds `sideEffectsCache.exclude` for packages whose builds depend on system libraries outside the cache key. [12.13](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.13.0) adds `pnpm profile` and `pnpm token`, plus a `storeIndexFormat: files` setting that replaces the SQLite store index with one file per package for stores shared over a network filesystem.

[mise 2026.10.8 to 2026.10.12](https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/tag/v2026.10.12) reads release lists, tags and attestations from its mise-versions host instead of `api.github.com`. A cold `mise install` of `github:` tools now makes no GitHub API requests, and `mise ls-remote python` went from 961 ms to 93 ms. [2026.10.9](https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/tag/v2026.10.9) fixes a trust bypass where an untrusted `path:` tool version could put a directory on `PATH`, and 2026.10.11 fixes a trust issue in remote task files.

[vlt 1.4.0](https://vlt.io/blog/vlt-1-4) turns the global store on by default on macOS, cloning packages with copy-on-write `clonefile` through `node:ffi` on Node 26.1 and later. A warm reinstall went from 9.6 s to 3.1 s. It also adds `--save-types`, which adds the matching `@types` package to devDependencies, and a [`vlt outdated`](https://vlt.io/blog/vlt-outdated) command whose JSON output includes the install command for each update.

[.NET 11 RC2](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/dotnet-11-rc-2/) adds `--min-publish-age-hours` to `dotnet nuget add source` and `dotnet nuget update source`, which writes the `minPublishAgeHours` setting to `nuget.config`. According to the [NuGet release notes](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc2/nuget.md), `dotnet package add` and `dotnet package update` apply the cooldown, and restoring a floating version fails with NU1020 when the cooldown excludes every matching version.

[pixi 0.82.0](https://github.com/prefix-dev/pixi/releases/tag/v0.82.0) adds `exclude-newer` to the `pixi global` manifest, taking a date or a duration such as `"7d"`, and accepts `amdgpu = true` or a specific GPU architecture such as `"gfx90a"` in platform declarations.

[sbt 2.1.0-RC1](https://github.com/sbt/sbt/releases/tag/v2.1.0-RC1) removes Apache Ivy from its dependencies and publishes without it. The metabuild moves to Scala 3.9, so plugins built for sbt 2.1 require sbt 2.1 or later.

[pipx 1.18](https://github.com/pypa/pipx/releases/tag/1.18.0) runs `upgrade-all`, `reinstall-all` and `install-all` across several environments at once, and masks passwords in index and package URLs in its output and logs. [1.18.2](https://github.com/pypa/pipx/releases/tag/1.18.2) accepts absolute file URLs for local package installs.

[uv 0.13.1](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/tag/0.13.1) reports missing trusted hashes in resolution errors and adds preliminary parsing of PEP 825 variant labels in wheel filenames behind the `wheel-variants` preview. Tool and managed Python uninstalls now delete only their own storage directories and leave files next to them in place.

[Spack Packages v2026.10.0](https://github.com/spack/spack-packages/releases/tag/v2026.10.0) has 9,095 packages, up from 8,752 in 2026.06.0, and deprecates versions of several packages to address CVEs. It uses the v2.2 Package API, which works with Spack 1.0.0 and later. Its binaries are published to a `releases/v2026.10` build cache mirror.

[Renovate 44.161 to 44.165](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.165.2) resolves Go modules whose `go-import` meta tag names a `mod` proxy as of [44.164.0](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/pull/47044), which covers generated modules from a private Buf Schema Registry. An Ubuntu libcurl security update in the 44.161.0 base image made git send username-only credentials on the first request of a clone and omit them from the follow-up. Self-hosted users with a personal access token [could no longer clone private repositories](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/discussions/47071). The fix in [44.164.1](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.164.1) puts the token after `x-access-token:` in GitHub clone URLs. [44.164.9](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/releases/tag/44.164.9) adds a fallback username for SCM-Manager and is the version the maintainers recommend upgrading to. In the configuration JSON Schema, [#46945](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate/pull/46945) limits known object properties to their listed keys.

[Dependabot Core 0.400.0](https://github.com/dependabot/dependabot-core/releases/tag/v0.400.0) adds an `apm` (Agent Package Manager) ecosystem and supports Bun 1.4 lockfiles. [zizmor 1.31](https://docs.zizmor.sh/release-notes/#1310) treats `issue_comment` as a dangerous trigger and flags `cache-mode: write` and `write-only` alongside dangerous triggers. `typosquat-uses` now also checks pre-commit inputs.

Also out:

  - [Rust 1.99.1](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/10/15/Rust-1.99.1/)

  - [npm 12.2.1](https://github.com/npm/cli/releases/tag/v12.2.1)

  - [conda 26.9.3](https://github.com/conda/conda/releases/tag/26.9.3)

  - [Nix 2.35.3](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/releases/tag/2.35.3)

  - [NuGet 8.1.0.12](https://github.com/NuGet/NuGet.Client/releases/tag/8.1.0.12)

  - [MacPorts 2.12.7](https://github.com/macports/macports-base/releases/tag/v2.12.7)

  - [Helm 4.3.1](https://github.com/helm/helm/releases/tag/v4.3.1)

  - [Helm 3.22.1](https://github.com/helm/helm/releases/tag/v3.22.1)

  - [Podman 6.1.4](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/releases/tag/v6.1.4)

  - [Podman 5.8.9](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/releases/tag/v5.8.9)

  - [Terraform 1.17.0-rc2](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/releases/tag/v1.17.0-rc2)

## Security

[Package managers have an integrity problem](https://blog.trailofbits.com/2026/10/14/package-managers-have-an-integrity-problem/) (Keegan Ryan, Trail of Bits) runs 25 package managers with default settings against a simulated compromised repository behind mitmproxy. Go and vcpkg were the two that verified every download when there was no lockfile, and Go alone verified signatures by default. Fewer than half check lockfile hashes for tampering by default. The post proposes recording signer identity in lockfiles, backed by Sigstore identity signing and a transparency log.

[rubygems.org now shows security warnings](https://blog.rubygems.org/2026/10/15/rubygems-org-now-shows-security-warnings-for-gems.html) (Anton Bondaronok) on gem version pages, using OSV data refreshed every hour. Reports from the OpenSSF Malicious Packages project are labelled as malware, and older affected versions get a warning icon in the versions list. For now the warnings appear on rubygems.org pages only, and the next step is adding advisory data to the Compact Index so `gem install` and `bundle install` can show them. [RubyGems 4.0.23](https://blog.rubygems.org/2026/10/14/4.0.23-released.html) drops setuid, setgid and sticky bits from files when it extracts a gem.

[PyPI now checks email reputation](https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2026-10-16-email-reputation-and-outlook/) when an address is used to register or is added to an account, and rejects disposable addresses using a service donated by UserCheck. In the past month the check blocked 62 disposable domains and more than 120 disposable addresses on otherwise valid domains. PyPI banned `outlook.com` and `hotmail.com` in June 2024 after a malware campaign used them to register accounts in bulk, and with the check in place both domains are accepted again.

[GitHub’s malware advisories now cover eight ecosystems](https://openssf.org/blog/2026/10/16/case-study-github-expands-malware-advisories-across-eight-ecosystems-with-openssf/) (OpenSSF), up from npm only to npm, PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, crates.io and Composer. GitHub imports reports from the [OpenSSF Malicious Packages](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) repository, which contains more than 238,000 reports in OSV format, and Dependabot users with malware alerts turned on get the wider coverage with their existing configuration.

[pnpm 12.12.1](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.12.1) and [11.28.6](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/11.28.6) make `pnpm publish` use an `NPM_ID_TOKEN` only when its `aud` claim matches the registry being published to, so a CI identity token goes only to the registry it was issued for. [12.12.0](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.12.0) makes an `allowBuilds` entry set to `false` take precedence over `dangerouslyAllowAllBuilds`, which previously ran those build scripts anyway.

[Hex 2.5.3](https://github.com/hexpm/hex/releases/tag/v2.5.3) fixes [CVE-2026-96596](https://github.com/erlang/otp/security/advisories/GHSA-phm5-m6cj-5382), where a GNU sparse file in a package or docs tarball could put `mix deps.get` into an infinite loop. It also percent-encodes package names and versions in request URLs, so a `/`, `?`, `#` or `..` stays inside its path segment.

[Docker Engine 29.9.1](https://github.com/moby/moby/releases/tag/docker-v29.9.1) updates containerd to 2.4.2 for three advisories where a malicious registry or crafted image could crash containerd or fill the host disk. [OpenTofu 1.12.8](https://github.com/opentofu/opentofu/releases/tag/v1.12.8) and [Terraform 1.16.6](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/releases/tag/v1.16.6) both fix excessive CPU usage when `init` connects to an attacker-controlled HTTP/2 server while installing dependencies, which Terraform’s notes track as CVE-2026-78669.

[How the PHP Security Team Handles Your Reports](https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/14/how-the-php-security-team-handles-your-reports/) (Alexandre Daubois, PHP Foundation) covers the triage process for php-src. Since 1 July the team has published 15 CVEs and closed 106 other reports as invalid, duplicates or not reproducible. Reports are reproduced on Linux, macOS and Windows under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. AI-written reports are accepted if the issue reproduces on a PHP build.

## Articles

[Nixpkgs for the frontend impaired](https://fzakaria.com/2026/10/12/nixpkgs-for-the-frontend-impaired) (Farid Zakaria) introduces [jinx](https://github.com/fzakaria/jinx), which compiles each `.nix` file to a TypeScript module. Across three platforms, 229,063 of nixpkgs’ 231,777 attributes produce the same drvPath as Nix, and the other 2,714 fail in both. It runs in Node 24 or a browser tab, three to five times slower than Nix. A second post, [Always, sometimes, never](https://fzakaria.com/2026/10/14/always-sometimes-never), adds property checks such as `single-writer` and `atomic-replace` to Rewind VM’s schedule exploration.

[Reproducible Builds in September 2026](https://reproducible-builds.org/reports/2026-09/) covers the summit in Gothenburg and seven proposals for the `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` specification that are open for feedback until 1 December. dettrace now runs on most Debian and openSUSE architectures and supports PGO builds.

[Thank you, Deno](https://vlt.io/blog/competition-keeps-javascript-moving) (Darcy Clarke, vlt), written after last week’s Cloudflare news, credits competition from Deno and Bun for features Node and npm later shipped, including `fetch`, the built-in test runner, type stripping and npm 12 making install scripts opt-in.

## Elsewhere

[Mend upgraded 184 open source organisations to the Renovate Community plan](https://www.mend.io/blog/renovate-community-oss-plan-upgrades/) (Jamie Tanna, Mend). The upgrade covers about 3,000 repositories on Mend-hosted Renovate, including Argo, Biome, Nuxt, Tauri and the Rust project. The plan raises resource limits and concurrency and adds Merge Confidence. Other projects can request it in a Mend Hosted Request discussion.

[VulnBump](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17374) (Gabija Pasiunaite et al., arXiv) is a benchmark from Snyk of 307 dependency upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers. A task passes when dependencies resolve and a rescan shows the fix, with the build and previously passing tests still green. Applying Snyk’s recommended version passed 46.9% of tasks, Claude Code on its own 59.6%, and Snyk’s remediation agent 90.2%.

[Forgejo 17.0](https://forgejo.org/2026-10-release-v17-0/) reads `FUNDING.yml` to show a Donate button on repositories and profiles, and adds LFS views for locks and pointer files, plus a list of the commits that changed each file. The project [recommends waiting before upgrading to 17.0.0](https://floss.social/@forgejo/117450533397721524) while it investigates an issue in that release that can stop pushes, merges and other code operations.

The [Python Packaging Council](https://discuss.python.org/t/python-packaging-council-has-a-github-repository/109533) has made its [GitHub repository](https://github.com/python/packaging-council) public, and will post the notes from each meeting there. People can file issues on the tracker to ask the council for a decision or for input.

## git-pkgs

I tagged [bibtex v0.1.0](https://github.com/git-pkgs/bibtex/releases/tag/v0.1.0) (new), a Go library for reading BibTeX such as `CITATION.bib` files and entries embedded in READMEs, built for scanning untrusted input in bulk, alongside [brief v0.14.2](https://github.com/git-pkgs/brief/releases/tag/v0.14.2) and [integrity v0.2.0](https://github.com/git-pkgs/integrity/releases/tag/v0.2.0).

## Israeli ad-tech company was a delivery system for "mercenary spyware" ([permalink](https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/17/mercenary-spyware/#discover-tech))

More than half of all internet users have installed an ad-blocker; Doc Searls calls it the largest consumer boycott in history. As large as that boycott is, everyone – yes, *everyone* – should block *every* "programmatic" ad, because the entire system is so insecure that failing to do so could result in the total compromise of any or all of your digital devices.

That's the inescapable conclusion of Citizen Lab's latest blockbuster investigative report, "Exposing AdFection," which reveals how the largest ad-tech companies in the world, including Google and Facebook, allowed themselves to be hijacked by a "mercenary spyware" company that used the ad system to locate targeted individuals and serve "zero-click malware" that took over their computers and phones without them having to take *any* action:

[https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/](https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/)

These tech giants amassed detailed surveillance dossiers on virtually every internet user, and they've assigned each of us unique, persistent identifiers, like a Social Security Number for spying. These companies *also* allow advertisers – or anyone pretending to be an advertiser – to serve blobs of code (which is all an ad is) to anyone based on those identifiers.

This allowed an Israeli spyware company called Discover-Tech (which masquerades as an ad-tech company) to sell totalitarian governments and sleazy corporate mercenaries the ability to pluck individual internet users out of the billions who log in every day and then serve "malicious ads" (that is, blobs of arbitrary code) to those targeted users. These malicious ads contained "no-click, zero-day" attacks, which meant that they exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities to take over devices without *any* user interaction. The mere act of loading a web-page or opening an app that relied on one of these gigantic ad-tech companies to serve ads was enough to compromise your device. No clicks needed, and no warning.

Among the targets of this attack campaign were the computers of workers at Al Jazeera. They were attacked with malware from the mercenary spyware company Candiru (which now calls itself "Integrity Labs" because irony is not dead). Beyond Candiru, Discover-Tech also facilitates attacks by numerous criminal mercenary spyware companies, serving ads on hundreds of thousands of sites and apps.

Discover-Tech was "certified" as a safe supplier by Google, Yandex, Microsoft, Beeswax (a division of Comcast) and IAB, the ad-tech industry's leading professional association. Ironically, Discover-Tech even attacked users by serving them malicious GDPR notices that appeared to let users opt out of commercial surveillance.

Because Discover-Tech was certified by all these industry bodies and firms, it had access to more than *four billion* ad-auctions, meaning that on *billions* of occasions, it was able to collect the identities of users loading apps and visiting websites, check them against the list of targets, and attack any victims it discovered through this dragnet.

Discover-Tech is an Israeli company with ties to other Israeli spyware and hacking companies, including through its board, whose members included Eric Banoun ("One of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel" –*Haaretz*). They have overlaps, relationships and affiliations with a rogue's gallery of Israeli companies, including the notorious NSO Group, who routinely sell cyber-weapons to the world's worst governments and whose products have been used to attack journalists, embassy workers, and activists.

The whole incident highlights the monumental insecurity of the ad-tech industry, whose indiscriminate and voracious surveillance and manifestly insufficient vetting and security auditing now exposes every internet user in the world to terrifying targeted attacks. These companies – including Google, a thrice-convicted monopolist whose surveillance tendrils are wrapped around the whole world – claim that they operate their networks with prudence and oversight. But the proof is in the pudding: for years, they've played host to a murderer's row of cyber-mercenaries who used their infrastructure to attack journalists and others.

The only way to avoid this is to block ads. This is easy enough to do in a browser (which is why the majority of internet users have installed an ad-blocker in their browsers), but it's *illegal* to reverse-engineer and modify an app so you can block the ads in it:

[https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element](https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/21/dickovers/#block-element)

Many websites run anti-ad-block scripts that push out nagging, guilt-tripping notices that call you a thief and a cheapskate for blocking ads. Ignore those notices: if a website is running "programmatic" ads that allow arbitrary third parties to spy on billions of people and target individuals for malicious device takeovers, they are charging too high a price to see their content.

Some sites go further: their notices demand that you either turn off your ad-blocker or pay for a subscription. This "pay or okay" scheme is illegal in Europe, California and other territories with strong privacy laws, and they are morally bankrupt besides. Privacy shouldn't be a luxury item and *everyone* deserves to be secure from cyber-attacks:

[https://noyb.eu/en/noybs-pay-or-okay-report-how-companies-make-you-pay-privacy](https://noyb.eu/en/noybs-pay-or-okay-report-how-companies-make-you-pay-privacy)

This report also provides the most comprehensive rebuttal to a dangerous idea that refuses to die: that we should improve competition in the ad-tech sector by assigning every internet user a mandatory, government-issued advertising ID to "democratize" ad-targeting and followup (which the sector calls "attribution"):

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/07/revealed-preferences/#extinguish-v-improve](https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/07/revealed-preferences/#extinguish-v-improve)

Despite all this, none of it is an indictment of ads *per se*. The problem here isn't *advertising*, it's *surveillance*. The ad-tech sector has convinced advertisers that targeting ads to *users* rather than *content* will massively improve ad performance. The evidence for this is *very* poor: targeted ads improve clickthrough rates by less than 5% (relative to content-based ads that relate to the substance of the page you're looking at), and they're incredibly expensive (and *very* dangerous!) to serve.

On top of all that, surveillance-based ads shift power away from publishers (who know more about the materials they publish than any ad-tech company ever will) to spying ad-tech companies (who can spy on users in ways that no publisher could ever match). Whatever minor additional revenues surveillance advertising can wring out of the market are totally swamped by the cost of the ad-tech sector's own operations, which the ad-tech sector makes up for by grossly underinvesting in security and by colluding to cheat publishers *and* advertisers, charging more for ads and paying less to the websites that run them:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue)

If we want to improve competition in advertising services, the answer isn't to facilitate spying (which also allows the world's scummiest cyber-mercenaries to stage and serve targeted attacks). We should ban surveillance advertising altogether, restoring context-based ads to their role as the way that publishers make an honest living without selling out their audiences:

[https://pluralistic.net/2023/05/31/context-ads/#class-formation](https://pluralistic.net/2023/05/31/context-ads/#class-formation)
